newsitem.title: USA: Local job growth firm, productivity up--Dallas Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local job growth firm, productivity up--Dallas Fed.

text.p: Strong job growth in the 11th U.S. economic district is outperforming the national average, bolstered by a robust economy and rising productivity, said an official at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.
"The economy here is very healthy, quite strong," Mine Yucel, a regional economist at the Dallas Fed, told Reuters. "It's been better than the national average ... as far as employment growth goes."

Recent data for the district, which encompasses Texas, northern Louisiana and southern New Mexico, showed that total private employment grew by an annualized rate of 3.1 percent in the second quarter of 1997, Yucel said.
Total private employment grew by an annualized 2.5 percent for the entire U.S. in the same period, she added.
Yucel said the local manufacturing sector, particularly the energy and high technology industries in Texas, have recently shown a spectacular performance.
She said the energy sector has managed to increase profits and boost final output despite an overall drop in oil prices.

"It's not really the price that is running it, it's the improvements in technology that are doing it ... Even with the turn in prices, people are profitable. The energy industry is very healthy," Yucel said.
The Dallas Fed economist said the technology industry itself, which had experienced some weakness last year, had also rebounded and was now performing very well.
"The semiconductor industry has come back ... it's growing quite well and there is a lot of labor market tightness in the high-tech sector. Supply is not meeting demand," Yucel said.

She said overall industry costs in the region have come down noticeably over the past few months due to productivity increases, which suggest that companies' massive investments in technology appear to have begun paying off.
Asked whether she saw any price pressures in the region, Yucel said, "We are not seeing any wage increases (and) even if we do see wage increases, we're not seeing price increases in the industries."

Productivity gains are a hot topic lately, as economists, including some at the Federal Reserve, look for signs the nation can continue to grow rapidly with low unemployment without sparking faster inflation.
The Dallas Fed economist also said the local construction sector was healthy. She added, however, that the sector's strength could ease somewhat towards the end of the year.

"The construction sector is also very strong ... it might level off toward the end of the year. There might be a slight slowing, but not something that is going to be called slow. It's moderating, but the growth is still high," she said.
On the consumer sector, the Dallas Fed economist said she had perceived local spending was showing some signs of tapering off.
Yucel added, however, that although consumer sales seemed to be moderating, retail employment had remained at lofty levels in the region.
The phenomenon, the economist added, could indicate retailer optimism regarding the future of the local economy.

"On the consumer side we've had signs of weakening retail sales. But this is on the sales side. Now if you look at retail sales employment, or retail trade employment, that has not come down. That is still quite strong," she said.
"Why are they still continuing to hire people? I guess they are all optimistic," she added.
The Dallas Fed is headed by Robert McTeer, a member of the central bank's policy setting Federal Open Market Committee.
McTeer is not scheduled to vote on policy action in 1997 given the committee's rotation rules.
The Fed last changed interest rates on March 25, when it bumped up the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent. The Fed stood pat during its May and July policy meetings.
